Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Assess characteristics of cavovarus foot deformity.
Outline imaging studies used to identify cavovarus foot deformity.
Compare the differences among idiopathic, traumatic, and neuromuscular cavovarus foot
deformities.
Definition and Overview
Cavus describes a high (abnormally elevated) longitudinal arch.
Varus describes hindfoot alignment toward the midline (medial to the anatomic axis).
The forefoot deformity is one of first-ray plantar flexion, often with forefoot adduction and
pronation.
The hindfoot deformity is one of calcaneal varus and increased calcaneal pitch.


Definition and Overview
Cavovarus is a term frequently misused to describe any foot with a high arch. However,
several components beyond cavus and varus must be considered, some but not all of
which may be present. The deformity also should be conceptualized in rotational and
osteologic frameworks, further increasing the understanding that cavovarus foot
deformity is more than just a high arch.
A cavovarus deformity, similar to pes planovalgus, may be a part of the normal spectrum
of foot architecture; however, recognition of even a mild idiopathic cavovarus foot is
critical in the management of several common foot and ankle disorders. A posttraumatic
or neurologic deformity typically is more easily recognized in the clinical setting but may
be progressive and pose more difficulty during management. More than one-half of all
cavovarus deformities result from underlying neurologic conditions. Therefore, a careful
patient history and physical examination are key to the treatment of these patients.
Diagnosis and Evaluation
Evaluation
Assessment of cavovarus deformity is based on a detailed patient history, physical
examination, and imaging studies.
Patient History
A family history may reveal similar problems in other family members because many
neurologic cavovarus feet arise from genetic diseases. Medical and family histories may be
critical in patients with symptoms that arise from a cavovarus foot, including chronic lateral
ankle instability, peroneal tendon pathology, and lateral column overload.

Physical Examination
In addition to a thorough neurologic examination, important clinical findings include
Standing hindfoot and ankle varus1 (Figure 1)
First metatarsal plantar flexion
Subtle cavus and peek-a-boo heel (the medial heel is visible during anterior inspection)
Asymmetric wear of the lateral shoe sole
Clawing of the toes, consistent with intrinsic muscle weakness

Forefoot-Driven Deformity
A cavovarus deformity may be forefoot driven or mixed. The deforming forces must be
understood to determine appropriate management. The Coleman block test eliminates
plantar flexion of the first ray as a driver of hindfoot varus. A 1-inch block (or book) is
placed under the patient’s heel and lateral foot, which offloads, or floats, the first
metatarsal head. Heel varus that corrects with the Coleman block test is forefoot driven,
and management should focus on addressing the plantar flexion of the first ray. Heel
varus that remains is then isolated to the hindfoot or driven by the hindfoot and
forefoot.2 (Figure 2).
Figure 2 Illustrations show the Coleman lateral block test as viewed from the front (A)
and the back (B). Note that the hindfoot varus corrects to neutral, indicating that the
cavovarus deformity is the result of a plantarflexed first ray. (Reproduced with
permission from Alexander IJ: Pes cavus, in Nunley JA, Pfeffer GB, Sanders RW, Trepman
E, eds: Advanced Reconstruction: Foot and Ankle. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2004, pp 495-502.)

Anatomy/Pathoanatomy

The tibialis anterior and peroneus brevis muscles typically are weak compared with the
peroneus longus and posterior tibialis muscles. This imbalance leads to plantar flexion of
the first ray and medial subluxation of the navicular on the talus. Claw toes may result
from relative weakness of the intrinsic foot musculature. Intrinsic weakness also may
contribute to the cavus deformity. These forces are described in Table 1.3

Etiology
A cavovarus deformity generally is idiopathic, traumatic, congenital, or neuromuscular.
Idiopathic

Idiopathic
The idiopathic cavovarus foot is pathologic only if it causes functional problems. It may
not be obvious on clinical examination (the subtle cavus foot). Recognition of even mild
cavovarus deformity in patients with other musculoskeletal diagnoses may be critical for
successful management. Diagnoses commonly observed in patients with a cavovarus
foot include:
Chronic lateral ankle instability
Peroneal tendon pathology
Fifth metatarsal stress fractures
Sesamoid disorders
Lateral column overload
Midfoot arthritis
Plantar fasciitis
Idiopathic cavovarus feet should be symmetric; nonprogressive; and, typically, less
pronounced than pathologic cavovarus deformities. Because the deformity may be
subtle, careful examination is warranted.
Traumatic

Traumatic

Although most cases are idiopathic or neuromuscular, the cavovarus foot also may
result from trauma. Injuries resulting in a cavovarus deformity include burns, crush
injuries, sequela of compartment syndrome, severe chronic lateral ankle instability and
peroneal insufficiency, and talus fracture malunion.
Congenital

Congenital
Cavovarus deformity also may be the result of congenital disease, namely arthrogryposis
and idiopathic clubfoot4 (Figure 7).
Figure 7 Clinical photographs of the feet of a 9.5-year-old girl with arthrogryposis show
severe congenital clubfoot. The patient previously underwent extensive clubfoot soft-
tissue releases; however, she experienced severe recurrence. A, Photograph of the right
foot obtained before cast immobilization. Dorsal (B) and plantar (C) view photographs of
bilateral feet obtained before cast immobilization show deep cavus, severe heel varus,
forefoot adductus, and supination. D, Photograph of bilateral feet obtained after eight
casts and bilateral percutaneous Achilles tenotomy, followed by another six casts and
transition to braces. Dorsal (E) and plantar (F) view photographs of the right foot and
posterior view photograph of bilateral feet obtained at the time the patient was aged 16
years (G). The patient underwent three series of cast immobilization during the previous
6 years. (Reproduced from Van Bosse HJP and Zlotolow DA: The orthopaedic

Neuromuscular

Neuromuscular
Two-thirds of cavovarus deformities are caused by an underlying neurologic diagnosis.
Accordingly, a neurologic examination is critical in the evaluation of the cavovarus foot.
The neuromuscular cavovarus deformity may be static or progressive and unilateral or
bilateral. Regardless of the underlying disorder, the pathoanatomy of deformity is the
result of the muscular imbalances described in Table 2. Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease
(hereditary sensory motor neuropathy) is the most common inherited neuropathy and
almost always results in bilateral deformity (Figure 8). A unilateral cavovarus foot may
result from various conditions, including poliomyelitis, cerebral palsy, stroke, Friedrich
ataxia, spinal cord lesions, and tumors. In the pediatric patient with a unilateral
deformity, advanced imaging studies are indicated to diagnose spinal anomalies (ie, a
tethered cord, syringomyelia).
